questions.subject: Criminal Law (BNS / IPC)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita / IPC (Sec. 378 IPC / Sec. 303 BNS)
questions.question: Q1. Dishonest intention at the time of taking movable property out of the possession of another without consent constitutes:

rectification.principle: Theft requires dishonest intention to take movable property out of another person possession without consent.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Criminal misappropriation and CBT involve lawful initial possession, whereas theft is unlawful taking from possession.
rectification.howToRectify: Check whether property was already entrusted (CBT) or taken without consent (Theft).

questions.subject: Criminal Law (BNS / IPC)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita / IPC (Sec. 499 IPC / Sec. 356 BNS)
questions.question: Q2. Which of the following is a valid statutory exception to criminal defamation?

options.label: A
options.text: Imputation made in private correspondence only

options.label: B
options.text: True imputation made for the public good

rectification.principle: Truth alone is not a complete defence in criminal defamation unless it is also made for the public good (First Exception).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: In civil defamation truth alone suffices, but criminal defamation requires truth + public good.
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize the dual test: Truth AND Public Good.

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure (BNSS / CrPC)
questions.statuteRef: BNSS / Code of Criminal Procedure (Sec. 154 CrPC / Sec. 173 BNSS)
questions.question: Q3. In Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of UP, registration of an FIR on receipt of information disclosing a cognizable offence was held to be:

rectification.principle: Registration of FIR is mandatory under Section 154 CrPC / 173 BNSS if information discloses commission of a cognizable offence.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Some exceptions allow preliminary inquiry (matrimonial, commercial, medical negligence), causing confusion about the general rule.
rectification.howToRectify: General rule = mandatory FIR; preliminary inquiry is only for narrow specified categories.

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure (BNSS / CrPC)
questions.statuteRef: BNSS / Code of Criminal Procedure (Sec. 167(2) CrPC / Sec. 187 BNSS)
questions.question: Q4. What is the maximum period of detention beyond which an accused is entitled to default bail when the offence is punishable with death or life imprisonment?

rectification.principle: Default/statutory bail accrues at 90 days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or 10+ years, and 60 days for other offences.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates frequently swap the 60-day and 90-day thresholds.
rectification.howToRectify: 90 days = >=10 years / life / death; 60 days = all other offences.

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure (BNSS / CrPC)
questions.statuteRef: BNSS / Code of Criminal Procedure (Sec. 438 CrPC / Sec. 482 BNSS)
questions.question: Q5. Which courts have concurrent jurisdiction to grant anticipatory bail?

options.label: A
options.text: Magistrate First Class and Sessions Court

options.label: B
options.text: High Court and Court of Session

rectification.principle: Only the High Court and the Court of Session may grant anticipatory bail under Sec. 438 CrPC / Sec. 482 BNSS.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Magistrates grant regular bail under Sec. 437/480, never anticipatory bail.
rectification.howToRectify: Anticipatory bail = Session Court or High Court only.

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure (BNSS / CrPC)
questions.statuteRef: BNSS / Code of Criminal Procedure (Sec. 482 CrPC / Sec. 528 BNSS)
questions.question: Q6. Inherent powers to prevent abuse of the process of any court or secure the ends of justice vest exclusively in the:

rectification.principle: Section 482 CrPC / Section 528 BNSS saves the inherent powers of the High Court alone.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Subordinate criminal courts have no inherent powers analogous to Sec. 151 CPC.
rectification.howToRectify: Compare Sec. 151 CPC (every civil court) vs Sec. 482 CrPC / 528 BNSS (High Court only).

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam / Evidence Act (Sec. 27 IEA / Sec. 23(2) BSA)
questions.question: Q7. How much of an information received from an accused in police custody is admissible when a fact is discovered in consequence?

options.label: B
options.text: Only so much of the information as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered

options.label: C
options.text: Only statements signed by two gazetted officers

options.label: D
options.text: None if made to a police officer

rectification.principle: Only the portion of information distinctly relating to the fact discovered is admissible as an exception to the bar on police confessions.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates mistake the rule as admitting the whole confessional narrative.
rectification.howToRectify: Recall Pulukuri Kottaya v. Emperor: only the discovery-linked portion is admissible.

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam / Evidence Act (Sec. 32(1) IEA / Sec. 26(a) BSA)
questions.question: Q8. A dying declaration is admissible in evidence under the principle:

rectification.principle: A person who is about to die is presumed not to lie (nemo moriturus praesumitur mentire).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Latin maxims are often tested directly in AIBE.
rectification.howToRectify: Pair dying declaration with nemo moriturus praesumitur mentire.

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam / Evidence Act (Sec. 115 IEA / Sec. 121 BSA)
questions.question: Q9. When one person has by declaration, act, or omission intentionally caused another to believe a thing to be true and act upon it, which rule applies?

rectification.principle: Section 115 IEA / 121 BSA codifies the rule of estoppel, preventing a party from denying a representation relied upon.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Estoppel (rule of evidence) is often confused with Res Judicata (rule of procedure).
rectification.howToRectify: Estoppel binds representations by a party; Res Judicata binds prior judicial decisions.

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam / Evidence Act (Sec. 65B IEA / Sec. 63 BSA)
questions.question: Q10. Admissibility of secondary electronic records requires a certificate as held mandatory in:

options.label: A
options.text: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal

options.label: B
options.text: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India

options.label: C
options.text: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India

options.label: D
options.text: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India

rectification.principle: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar (2020) affirmed that a Sec. 65B(4) certificate is a mandatory condition precedent for secondary electronic evidence.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Earlier conflicting rulings (Shafhi Mohammad) caused confusion before Arjun Panditrao settled the law.
rectification.howToRectify: Associate Sec. 65B(4) / Sec. 63 BSA certificate with Arjun Panditrao Khotkar.

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.statuteRef: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Sec. 11 CPC)
questions.question: Q11. The doctrine of Res Judicata under Section 11 CPC applies when:

options.label: A
options.text: An earlier suit is still pending

options.label: B
options.text: A matter directly and substantially in issue has been heard and finally decided by a competent court

options.label: D
options.text: A suit is withdrawn with liberty

rectification.principle: Section 11 bars re-litigation of matters directly and substantially in issue between the same parties after final adjudication on merits.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Pending earlier suits trigger Section 10 (Res Sub Judice), not Section 11.
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 10 = Stay of pending subsequent suit; Sec. 11 = Bar after final decision.

questions.statuteRef: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Order XXXIX Rules 1-2 CPC)
questions.question: Q12. Which three-pronged test governs the grant of a temporary injunction under Order 39 CPC?

options.label: B
options.text: Prima facie case, Balance of convenience, Irreparable injury

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.statuteRef: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Sec. 80 CPC)
questions.question: Q13. Before instituting a suit against the Government or a public officer for an official act, a statutory notice period of how many months is required?

rectification.principle: Section 80 CPC mandates a 2-month prior written notice before suing the Government or public officer, subject to urgent leave under Sec. 80(2).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Statutory notice durations differ across Acts (e.g., 2 months in CPC vs 30 days in NI Act).
rectification.howToRectify: Section 80 CPC = 2 months written notice.

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.statuteRef: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Order VII Rule 11 CPC)
questions.question: Q14. Rejection of a plaint on the ground that it does not disclose a cause of action is governed by:

rectification.principle: Order VII Rule 11 sets out the six mandatory grounds for rejection of a plaint, including lack of cause of action and statutory bar.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Order VI Rule 17 deals with amendment of pleadings, not rejection.
rectification.howToRectify: Order VII Rule 11 = Rejection of plaint (deemed decree under Sec. 2(2)).

questions.subject: Law of Contract & Specific Relief
questions.statuteRef: Indian Contract Act, 1872 / SRA 1963 (Sec. 11 ICA)
questions.question: Q15. In Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose, an agreement entered into by a minor was held to be:

rectification.principle: Under Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, a minor is incompetent to contract, rendering any minor agreement void ab initio.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Unlike coercion or undue influence (voidable), minority makes an agreement void from inception.
rectification.howToRectify: Minors agreements are void ab initio and cannot be ratified.

questions.subject: Law of Contract & Specific Relief
questions.statuteRef: Indian Contract Act, 1872 / SRA 1963 (Sec. 73 ICA)
questions.question: Q16. The rule in Hadley v. Baxendale regarding remoteness of damages is codified in India under:

rectification.principle: Section 73 awards compensation for loss arising naturally in the usual course of things or known to parties as likely to result from breach.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Section 74 deals with liquidated damages/penalty, whereas Section 73 states the general remoteness principle.
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 73 = Unliquidated damages (Hadley v. Baxendale); Sec. 74 = Stipulated sum/penalty.

questions.subject: Law of Contract & Specific Relief
questions.statuteRef: Indian Contract Act, 1872 / SRA 1963 (Sec. 56 ICA)
questions.question: Q17. When an agreement becomes impossible or unlawful to perform after it is made due to an unforeseen supervening event, it becomes void under:

rectification.principle: Section 56 second paragraph renders a contract void upon supervening impossibility or illegality (Doctrine of Frustration).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Commercial hardship alone does not trigger Sec. 56; physical or legal impossibility is required.
rectification.howToRectify: Recall Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur on Section 56.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.statuteRef: Hindu Marriage Act / Muslim Law / Succession (Sec. 13B HMA)
questions.question: Q18. Under Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, what is the minimum period of separate living required before filing a petition for divorce by mutual consent?

rectification.principle: Parties must have been living separately for a period of one year or more before presenting a Sec. 13B(1) mutual consent petition.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates confuse the 1-year pre-filing separation with the 6-month cooling-off motion period under Sec. 13B(2).
rectification.howToRectify: 1 year separation before filing; 6 to 18 months window for second motion (waivable per Amardeep Singh).

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.statuteRef: Hindu Marriage Act / Muslim Law / Succession (Sec. 6 HSA 1956 (2005 Amend.))
questions.question: Q19. In Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020), the Supreme Court held that a daughter becomes a coparcener by birth:

options.label: A
options.text: Only if her father was alive on 09.09.2005

options.label: B
options.text: Irrespective of whether her father was alive on 09.09.2005

rectification.principle: Daughters hold coparcenary status by birth with equal rights and liabilities regardless of whether the father was alive on 09-09-2005.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Earlier conflicting decisions (Prakash v. Phulavati) required the father to be alive in 2005.
rectification.howToRectify: Vineeta Sharma overruled Prakash v. Phulavati: coparcenary right is by birth.

questions.subject: Professional Ethics & BCI Rules
questions.statuteRef: Advocates Act, 1961 & BCI Rules (Sec. 35 Advocates Act)
questions.question: Q20. Complaints of professional or other misconduct against an advocate are heard in the first instance by:

options.label: B
options.text: The Disciplinary Committee of the State Bar Council

rectification.principle: Under Section 35 of the Advocates Act, the State Bar Council refers misconduct complaints to its Disciplinary Committee.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: BCI hears appeals under Sec. 37 and original complaints only on transfer/revision.
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 35 = State Bar Council DC; Sec. 37 = Appeal to BCI; Sec. 38 = Appeal to Supreme Court.

questions.subject: Professional Ethics & BCI Rules
questions.statuteRef: Advocates Act, 1961 & BCI Rules (Rule 36 BCI Standards)
questions.question: Q21. Under Rule 36 of the Bar Council of India Rules, an advocate is prohibited from:

options.label: A
options.text: Maintaining a factual website with prior intimation

options.label: B
options.text: Soliciting work or advertising directly or indirectly

rectification.principle: Rule 36 prohibits advocates from soliciting work or advertising, subject to the narrow 2008 amendment permitting basic website particulars.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates overlook the distinction between permitted factual website listings and prohibited solicitation.
rectification.howToRectify: Rule 36 = Strict ban on solicitation and commercial advertising.

questions.subject: Law of Torts & Consumer Protection
questions.statuteRef: Law of Torts / Motor Vehicles / CPA 2019 (M.C. Mehta Rule)
questions.question: Q22. In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak), the Supreme Court evolved the principle of Absolute Liability, which differs from Rylands v. Fletcher because:

options.label: A
options.text: It applies only to public sector units

options.label: B
options.text: It admits no exceptions such as Act of God or third-party act

options.label: C
options.text: It limits compensation to statutory caps

rectification.principle: Absolute Liability holds enterprises engaged in hazardous or inherently dangerous activities strictly liable with zero exceptions.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Strict liability (Rylands) allows exceptions like vis major; Absolute Liability allows none.
rectification.howToRectify: Absolute Liability = Strict Liability minus all Rylands v. Fletcher exceptions.

questions.subject: Law of Torts & Consumer Protection
questions.statuteRef: Law of Torts / Motor Vehicles / CPA 2019 (CPA 2019 Sec. 34)
questions.question: Q23. Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the District Commission has pecuniary jurisdiction where the value of goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed:

rectification.principle: Under the 2021 Rules notified under CPA 2019, District Commission jurisdiction is up to Rs. 50 Lakhs (State: 50L to 2 Cr; National: above 2 Cr).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: CPA 1986 limits (20L) and original 2019 Act text (1 Cr) were revised by the 2021 Pecuniary Jurisdiction Rules.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember revised 2021 limits: District <= 50L; State > 50L to 2 Cr; National > 2 Cr (based on consideration paid).

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.statuteRef: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (Sec. 34 A&C Act)
questions.question: Q24. What is the standard limitation period for filing an application to set aside an arbitral award under Section 34(3)?

options.label: C
options.text: 3 months (extendable by 30 days on sufficient cause)

rectification.principle: Section 34(3) prescribes 3 months from receipt of the award, extendable by at most 30 days on sufficient cause, but not thereafter (Sec. 5 Limitation Act excluded).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates confuse 3 months with 90 days or assume Section 5 Limitation Act applies indefinitely.
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 34(3): 3 months + max 30 days grace; Popular Construction excludes Sec. 5 Limitation Act.

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.statuteRef: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (Sec. 9 A&C Act)
questions.question: Q25. Interim measures before, during, or after arbitral proceedings (prior to enforcement) may be sought from a Court under:

rectification.principle: Section 9 empowers the Court to grant interim measures, whereas Section 17 empowers the Arbitral Tribunal.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Sec. 9 (Court) and Sec. 17 (Tribunal) are frequently swapped.
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 9 = Court interim relief; Sec. 17 = Tribunal interim relief.

questions.subject: Company Law & Commercial Laws
questions.statuteRef: Companies Act, 2013 / NI Act, 1881 (Sec. 138 NI Act)
questions.question: Q26. After receipt of a cheque dishonour demand notice under Section 138(b) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, how many days does the drawer have to make payment?

rectification.principle: Sec. 138(c) grants the drawer 15 days from receipt of notice to pay, failing which the cause of action accrues for filing a complaint within 1 month.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: 30 days is for issuing the notice after bank return memo; 15 days is for the drawer to pay.
rectification.howToRectify: Timeline: 30 days (payee sends notice) -> 15 days (drawer pays) -> 1 month (file complaint).

questions.subject: Company Law & Commercial Laws
questions.statuteRef: Companies Act, 2013 / NI Act, 1881 (Sec. 2(62) Companies Act)
questions.question: Q27. In Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd., the House of Lords established which foundational principle of Company Law?

rectification.principle: Upon incorporation, a company becomes a distinct legal entity separate from its shareholders and directors.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates confuse the default rule (separate personality) with its exception (veil lifting).
rectification.howToRectify: Salomon = Separate Legal Entity; Royal British Bank v. Turquand = Indoor Management.

questions.question: Q28. The maxim Nemo judex in causa sua embodies which pillar of natural justice?

questions.subject: Environmental & Labour Laws
questions.statuteRef: Environment Protection Act / ID Act (Vellore Citizens Case)
questions.question: Q29. Which principle requires that where there are threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage, lack of full scientific certainty shall not postpone cost-effective measures?

rectification.principle: The Precautionary Principle shifts the burden onto the developer/industrialist to show actions are environmentally benign.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Polluter Pays fixes financial liability after harm, whereas Precautionary Principle prevents irreversible harm ex ante.
rectification.howToRectify: Precautionary = Prevent before harm; Polluter Pays = Remediate and compensate after/for pollution.

questions.subject: Environmental & Labour Laws
questions.statuteRef: Environment Protection Act / ID Act (Sec. 25F ID Act)
questions.question: Q30. Before retrenching a workman who has been in continuous service for not less than one year, an employer must generally give:

options.label: B
options.text: 1 month notice or wages in lieu + retrenchment compensation

rectification.principle: Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act mandates 1 month written notice (or pay in lieu) plus 15 days average pay per completed year of continuous service.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Sec. 25F (1 month, <100 workers) differs from Sec. 25N (3 months + govt permission for >=100 workers).
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 25F = 1 month notice + 15 days pay/year; Sec. 25N = 3 months + prior government permission.

questions.subject: Taxation & Intellectual Property
questions.statuteRef: Income Tax Act / Patents & Trade Marks (Sec. 3(d) Patents Act)
questions.question: Q31. In Novartis AG v. Union of India, the Supreme Court interpreted Section 3(d) of the Patents Act, 1970 to prevent:

options.label: B
options.text: Evergreening of pharmaceutical patents without enhanced efficacy

rectification.principle: Section 3(d) bars patenting new forms of known substances unless they demonstrate significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates confuse evergreening (Sec. 3(d)) with compulsory licensing (Sec. 84).
rectification.howToRectify: Novartis = Sec. 3(d) anti-evergreening & therapeutic efficacy.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.statuteRef: Constitution of India (Art. 14)
questions.question: Q32. Which doctrine under Article 14 prohibits arbitrary state action and requires intelligible differentia with rational nexus?

rectification.principle: Article 14 permits reasonable classification based on intelligible differentia having a rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates often confuse Article 14 tests with legislative competence doctrines under Article 246.
rectification.howToRectify: Revise State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar and E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu on Article 14.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.statuteRef: Constitution of India (Art. 21)
questions.question: Q33. In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, the Supreme Court held that procedure established by law under Article 21 must be:

rectification.principle: Article 21 requires any procedure depriving life or personal liberty to be fair, just, and reasonable, not fanciful or oppressive.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Older pre-1978 Gopalan readings treated procedure as purely formal.
rectification.howToRectify: Anchor Article 21 with Articles 14 and 19 (the Golden Triangle).

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.statuteRef: Constitution of India (Art. 32)
questions.question: Q34. Which writ is issued by a Constitutional Court to quash an order passed without jurisdiction or in violation of natural justice?

rectification.principle: Certiorari is issued to quash orders of inferior courts or tribunals acting without or in excess of jurisdiction.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Certiorari (post-order quashing) is frequently mixed up with Prohibition (pre-order restraint).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: Prohibition prevents; Certiorari cures/quashes.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.statuteRef: Constitution of India (Art. 136)
questions.question: Q35. Special Leave to Appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 136 is:

options.label: D
options.text: Available only against High Court decrees

rectification.principle: Article 136 confers plenary discretionary power on the Supreme Court to grant special leave against any judgment, decree, or order of any court or tribunal in India.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates confuse Article 136 with regular appellate jurisdiction under Articles 132-134.
rectification.howToRectify: Note that military tribunals are the only exclusion under Article 136(2).

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.statuteRef: Constitution of India (Art. 368)
questions.question: Q36. Which judgment established that Parliament cannot alter the Basic Structure of the Constitution under Article 368?

options.label: B
options.text: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala

options.label: C
options.text: Minerva Mills v. Union of India

options.label: D
options.text: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India

rectification.principle: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) propounded the Basic Structure doctrine limiting amending power under Article 368.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Golaknath barred amending Fundamental Rights altogether, whereas Kesavananda introduced Basic Structure.
rectification.howToRectify: Link 1973 Kesavananda Bharati to Article 368 limits.

questions.subject: Criminal Law (BNS / IPC)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita / IPC (Sec. 34 IPC / Sec. 3(5) BNS)
questions.question: Q37. What is the essential requirement for fastening vicarious criminal liability under common intention?

options.label: B
options.text: Prior meeting of minds and participation in criminal act

rectification.principle: Common intention requires pre-arranged plan or prior meeting of minds plus participation in furtherance of that intention.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates mix up common intention (2+ persons) with unlawful assembly common object (5+ persons).
rectification.howToRectify: Compare Sec. 34 (common intention, active participation) with Sec. 149 (common object, 5+ members).

questions.subject: Criminal Law (BNS / IPC)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita / IPC (Sec. 300 IPC / Sec. 101 BNS)
questions.question: Q38. When does culpable homicide NOT amount to murder under the Exception of Grave and Sudden Provocation?

options.label: B
options.text: When the offender is deprived of self-control by grave and sudden provocation not sought as an excuse

options.label: D
options.text: When committed with a licensed weapon

rectification.principle: Exception 1 reduces murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder if the accused loses self-control due to grave and sudden provocation, subject to the three provisos.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Missing the provisos (not sought, not lawful exercise of public power/self-defence) leads to wrong choices.
rectification.howToRectify: Read K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra for the cooling-off time test.

rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Subordinate criminal courts have no inherent powers analogous to Sec. 151 CPC.
rectification.howToRectify: Compare Sec. 151 CPC (every civil court) vs Sec. 482 CrPC / 528 BNSS (High Court only).

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam / Evidence Act (Sec. 27 IEA / Sec. 23(2) BSA)
questions.question: Q45. How much of an information received from an accused in police custody is admissible when a fact is discovered in consequence?

options.label: B
options.text: Only so much of the information as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered

options.label: C
options.text: Only statements signed by two gazetted officers

options.label: D
options.text: None if made to a police officer

rectification.principle: This question was officially withdrawn by the Bar Council of India in the Final Answer Key.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Ambiguous statutory framing or multiple incompatible options led BCI to drop this item from scoring.
rectification.howToRectify: Withdrawn questions are excluded from the denominator (95 total scored marks). Focus on Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam / Evidence Act (Sec. 27 IEA / Sec. 23(2) BSA).

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam / Evidence Act (Sec. 32(1) IEA / Sec. 26(a) BSA)
questions.question: Q46. A dying declaration is admissible in evidence under the principle:

rectification.principle: A person who is about to die is presumed not to lie (nemo moriturus praesumitur mentire).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Latin maxims are often tested directly in AIBE.
rectification.howToRectify: Pair dying declaration with nemo moriturus praesumitur mentire.

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam / Evidence Act (Sec. 115 IEA / Sec. 121 BSA)
questions.question: Q47. When one person has by declaration, act, or omission intentionally caused another to believe a thing to be true and act upon it, which rule applies?

rectification.principle: Section 115 IEA / 121 BSA codifies the rule of estoppel, preventing a party from denying a representation relied upon.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Estoppel (rule of evidence) is often confused with Res Judicata (rule of procedure).
rectification.howToRectify: Estoppel binds representations by a party; Res Judicata binds prior judicial decisions.

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam / Evidence Act (Sec. 65B IEA / Sec. 63 BSA)
questions.question: Q48. Admissibility of secondary electronic records requires a certificate as held mandatory in:

options.label: A
options.text: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal

options.label: B
options.text: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India

options.label: C
options.text: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India

options.label: D
options.text: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India

rectification.principle: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar (2020) affirmed that a Sec. 65B(4) certificate is a mandatory condition precedent for secondary electronic evidence.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Earlier conflicting rulings (Shafhi Mohammad) caused confusion before Arjun Panditrao settled the law.
rectification.howToRectify: Associate Sec. 65B(4) / Sec. 63 BSA certificate with Arjun Panditrao Khotkar.

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.statuteRef: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Sec. 11 CPC)
questions.question: Q49. The doctrine of Res Judicata under Section 11 CPC applies when:

options.label: A
options.text: An earlier suit is still pending

options.label: B
options.text: A matter directly and substantially in issue has been heard and finally decided by a competent court

options.label: D
options.text: A suit is withdrawn with liberty

rectification.principle: Section 11 bars re-litigation of matters directly and substantially in issue between the same parties after final adjudication on merits.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Pending earlier suits trigger Section 10 (Res Sub Judice), not Section 11.
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 10 = Stay of pending subsequent suit; Sec. 11 = Bar after final decision.

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.statuteRef: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Order XXXIX Rules 1-2 CPC)
questions.question: Q50. Which three-pronged test governs the grant of a temporary injunction under Order 39 CPC?

options.label: B
options.text: Prima facie case, Balance of convenience, Irreparable injury

rectification.principle: Civil courts evaluate prima facie case, balance of convenience, and irreparable injury before granting temporary injunction.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates occasionally include irrelevant factors like solvency or finality.
rectification.howToRectify: Always check the triad: Prima facie case + Balance of convenience + Irreparable loss.

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.statuteRef: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Sec. 80 CPC)
questions.question: Q51. Before instituting a suit against the Government or a public officer for an official act, a statutory notice period of how many months is required?

rectification.principle: Section 80 CPC mandates a 2-month prior written notice before suing the Government or public officer, subject to urgent leave under Sec. 80(2).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Statutory notice durations differ across Acts (e.g., 2 months in CPC vs 30 days in NI Act).
rectification.howToRectify: Section 80 CPC = 2 months written notice.

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.statuteRef: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Order VII Rule 11 CPC)
questions.question: Q52. Rejection of a plaint on the ground that it does not disclose a cause of action is governed by:

rectification.principle: Order VII Rule 11 sets out the six mandatory grounds for rejection of a plaint, including lack of cause of action and statutory bar.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Order VI Rule 17 deals with amendment of pleadings, not rejection.
rectification.howToRectify: Order VII Rule 11 = Rejection of plaint (deemed decree under Sec. 2(2)).

questions.subject: Law of Contract & Specific Relief
questions.statuteRef: Indian Contract Act, 1872 / SRA 1963 (Sec. 11 ICA)
questions.question: Q53. In Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose, an agreement entered into by a minor was held to be:

rectification.principle: Under Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, a minor is incompetent to contract, rendering any minor agreement void ab initio.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Unlike coercion or undue influence (voidable), minority makes an agreement void from inception.
rectification.howToRectify: Minors agreements are void ab initio and cannot be ratified.

questions.subject: Law of Contract & Specific Relief
questions.statuteRef: Indian Contract Act, 1872 / SRA 1963 (Sec. 73 ICA)
questions.question: Q54. The rule in Hadley v. Baxendale regarding remoteness of damages is codified in India under:

rectification.principle: Section 73 awards compensation for loss arising naturally in the usual course of things or known to parties as likely to result from breach.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Section 74 deals with liquidated damages/penalty, whereas Section 73 states the general remoteness principle.
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 73 = Unliquidated damages (Hadley v. Baxendale); Sec. 74 = Stipulated sum/penalty.

questions.subject: Law of Contract & Specific Relief
questions.statuteRef: Indian Contract Act, 1872 / SRA 1963 (Sec. 56 ICA)
questions.question: Q55. When an agreement becomes impossible or unlawful to perform after it is made due to an unforeseen supervening event, it becomes void under:

rectification.principle: Section 56 second paragraph renders a contract void upon supervening impossibility or illegality (Doctrine of Frustration).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Commercial hardship alone does not trigger Sec. 56; physical or legal impossibility is required.
rectification.howToRectify: Recall Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur on Section 56.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.statuteRef: Hindu Marriage Act / Muslim Law / Succession (Sec. 13B HMA)
questions.question: Q56. Under Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, what is the minimum period of separate living required before filing a petition for divorce by mutual consent?

rectification.principle: Parties must have been living separately for a period of one year or more before presenting a Sec. 13B(1) mutual consent petition.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates confuse the 1-year pre-filing separation with the 6-month cooling-off motion period under Sec. 13B(2).
rectification.howToRectify: 1 year separation before filing; 6 to 18 months window for second motion (waivable per Amardeep Singh).

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.statuteRef: Hindu Marriage Act / Muslim Law / Succession (Sec. 6 HSA 1956 (2005 Amend.))
questions.question: Q57. In Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020), the Supreme Court held that a daughter becomes a coparcener by birth:

options.label: A
options.text: Only if her father was alive on 09.09.2005

options.label: B
options.text: Irrespective of whether her father was alive on 09.09.2005

rectification.principle: Daughters hold coparcenary status by birth with equal rights and liabilities regardless of whether the father was alive on 09-09-2005.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Earlier conflicting decisions (Prakash v. Phulavati) required the father to be alive in 2005.
rectification.howToRectify: Vineeta Sharma overruled Prakash v. Phulavati: coparcenary right is by birth.

questions.subject: Professional Ethics & BCI Rules
questions.statuteRef: Advocates Act, 1961 & BCI Rules (Sec. 35 Advocates Act)
questions.question: Q58. Complaints of professional or other misconduct against an advocate are heard in the first instance by:

options.label: B
options.text: The Disciplinary Committee of the State Bar Council

rectification.principle: Under Section 35 of the Advocates Act, the State Bar Council refers misconduct complaints to its Disciplinary Committee.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: BCI hears appeals under Sec. 37 and original complaints only on transfer/revision.
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 35 = State Bar Council DC; Sec. 37 = Appeal to BCI; Sec. 38 = Appeal to Supreme Court.

questions.subject: Professional Ethics & BCI Rules
questions.statuteRef: Advocates Act, 1961 & BCI Rules (Rule 36 BCI Standards)
questions.question: Q59. Under Rule 36 of the Bar Council of India Rules, an advocate is prohibited from:

options.label: A
options.text: Maintaining a factual website with prior intimation

options.label: B
options.text: Soliciting work or advertising directly or indirectly

rectification.principle: Rule 36 prohibits advocates from soliciting work or advertising, subject to the narrow 2008 amendment permitting basic website particulars.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates overlook the distinction between permitted factual website listings and prohibited solicitation.
rectification.howToRectify: Rule 36 = Strict ban on solicitation and commercial advertising.

questions.subject: Law of Torts & Consumer Protection
questions.statuteRef: Law of Torts / Motor Vehicles / CPA 2019 (M.C. Mehta Rule)
questions.question: Q60. In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak), the Supreme Court evolved the principle of Absolute Liability, which differs from Rylands v. Fletcher because:

options.label: A
options.text: It applies only to public sector units

options.label: B
options.text: It admits no exceptions such as Act of God or third-party act

options.label: C
options.text: It limits compensation to statutory caps

rectification.principle: Absolute Liability holds enterprises engaged in hazardous or inherently dangerous activities strictly liable with zero exceptions.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Strict liability (Rylands) allows exceptions like vis major; Absolute Liability allows none.
rectification.howToRectify: Absolute Liability = Strict Liability minus all Rylands v. Fletcher exceptions.

questions.subject: Law of Torts & Consumer Protection
questions.statuteRef: Law of Torts / Motor Vehicles / CPA 2019 (CPA 2019 Sec. 34)
questions.question: Q61. Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the District Commission has pecuniary jurisdiction where the value of goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed:

rectification.principle: Under the 2021 Rules notified under CPA 2019, District Commission jurisdiction is up to Rs. 50 Lakhs (State: 50L to 2 Cr; National: above 2 Cr).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: CPA 1986 limits (20L) and original 2019 Act text (1 Cr) were revised by the 2021 Pecuniary Jurisdiction Rules.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember revised 2021 limits: District <= 50L; State > 50L to 2 Cr; National > 2 Cr (based on consideration paid).

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.statuteRef: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (Sec. 34 A&C Act)
questions.question: Q62. What is the standard limitation period for filing an application to set aside an arbitral award under Section 34(3)?

options.label: C
options.text: 3 months (extendable by 30 days on sufficient cause)

rectification.principle: Section 34(3) prescribes 3 months from receipt of the award, extendable by at most 30 days on sufficient cause, but not thereafter (Sec. 5 Limitation Act excluded).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates confuse 3 months with 90 days or assume Section 5 Limitation Act applies indefinitely.
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 34(3): 3 months + max 30 days grace; Popular Construction excludes Sec. 5 Limitation Act.

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.statuteRef: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (Sec. 9 A&C Act)
questions.question: Q63. Interim measures before, during, or after arbitral proceedings (prior to enforcement) may be sought from a Court under:

rectification.principle: Section 9 empowers the Court to grant interim measures, whereas Section 17 empowers the Arbitral Tribunal.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Sec. 9 (Court) and Sec. 17 (Tribunal) are frequently swapped.
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 9 = Court interim relief; Sec. 17 = Tribunal interim relief.

questions.subject: Company Law & Commercial Laws
questions.statuteRef: Companies Act, 2013 / NI Act, 1881 (Sec. 138 NI Act)
questions.question: Q64. After receipt of a cheque dishonour demand notice under Section 138(b) of the Negotiable Instruments Act, how many days does the drawer have to make payment?

rectification.principle: Sec. 138(c) grants the drawer 15 days from receipt of notice to pay, failing which the cause of action accrues for filing a complaint within 1 month.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: 30 days is for issuing the notice after bank return memo; 15 days is for the drawer to pay.
rectification.howToRectify: Timeline: 30 days (payee sends notice) -> 15 days (drawer pays) -> 1 month (file complaint).

questions.subject: Company Law & Commercial Laws
questions.statuteRef: Companies Act, 2013 / NI Act, 1881 (Sec. 2(62) Companies Act)
questions.question: Q65. In Salomon v. A. Salomon & Co. Ltd., the House of Lords established which foundational principle of Company Law?

rectification.principle: Upon incorporation, a company becomes a distinct legal entity separate from its shareholders and directors.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates confuse the default rule (separate personality) with its exception (veil lifting).
rectification.howToRectify: Salomon = Separate Legal Entity; Royal British Bank v. Turquand = Indoor Management.

questions.subject: Administrative Law
questions.statuteRef: Principles of Administrative Law (Natural Justice)
questions.question: Q66. The maxim Nemo judex in causa sua embodies which pillar of natural justice?

rectification.principle: No person shall be a judge in their own cause, barring pecuniary, personal, or official bias.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Audi alteram partem (fair hearing) and Nemo judex (no bias) are sometimes swapped.
rectification.howToRectify: Nemo judex = No bias; Audi alteram partem = Hear the other side.

questions.subject: Environmental & Labour Laws
questions.statuteRef: Environment Protection Act / ID Act (Vellore Citizens Case)
questions.question: Q67. Which principle requires that where there are threats of serious or irreversible environmental damage, lack of full scientific certainty shall not postpone cost-effective measures?

rectification.principle: This question was officially withdrawn by the Bar Council of India in the Final Answer Key.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Ambiguous statutory framing or multiple incompatible options led BCI to drop this item from scoring.
rectification.howToRectify: Withdrawn questions are excluded from the denominator (95 total scored marks). Focus on Environment Protection Act / ID Act (Vellore Citizens Case).

questions.subject: Environmental & Labour Laws
questions.statuteRef: Environment Protection Act / ID Act (Sec. 25F ID Act)
questions.question: Q68. Before retrenching a workman who has been in continuous service for not less than one year, an employer must generally give:

options.label: B
options.text: 1 month notice or wages in lieu + retrenchment compensation

rectification.principle: Section 25F of the Industrial Disputes Act mandates 1 month written notice (or pay in lieu) plus 15 days average pay per completed year of continuous service.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Sec. 25F (1 month, <100 workers) differs from Sec. 25N (3 months + govt permission for >=100 workers).
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 25F = 1 month notice + 15 days pay/year; Sec. 25N = 3 months + prior government permission.

questions.subject: Taxation & Intellectual Property
questions.statuteRef: Income Tax Act / Patents & Trade Marks (Sec. 3(d) Patents Act)
questions.question: Q69. In Novartis AG v. Union of India, the Supreme Court interpreted Section 3(d) of the Patents Act, 1970 to prevent:

options.label: B
options.text: Evergreening of pharmaceutical patents without enhanced efficacy

rectification.principle: Section 3(d) bars patenting new forms of known substances unless they demonstrate significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates confuse evergreening (Sec. 3(d)) with compulsory licensing (Sec. 84).
rectification.howToRectify: Novartis = Sec. 3(d) anti-evergreening & therapeutic efficacy.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.statuteRef: Constitution of India (Art. 14)
questions.question: Q70. Which doctrine under Article 14 prohibits arbitrary state action and requires intelligible differentia with rational nexus?

rectification.principle: Article 14 permits reasonable classification based on intelligible differentia having a rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates often confuse Article 14 tests with legislative competence doctrines under Article 246.
rectification.howToRectify: Revise State of West Bengal v. Anwar Ali Sarkar and E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu on Article 14.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.statuteRef: Constitution of India (Art. 21)
questions.question: Q71. In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India, the Supreme Court held that procedure established by law under Article 21 must be:

rectification.principle: Article 21 requires any procedure depriving life or personal liberty to be fair, just, and reasonable, not fanciful or oppressive.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Older pre-1978 Gopalan readings treated procedure as purely formal.
rectification.howToRectify: Anchor Article 21 with Articles 14 and 19 (the Golden Triangle).

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.statuteRef: Constitution of India (Art. 32)
questions.question: Q72. Which writ is issued by a Constitutional Court to quash an order passed without jurisdiction or in violation of natural justice?

rectification.principle: Certiorari is issued to quash orders of inferior courts or tribunals acting without or in excess of jurisdiction.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Certiorari (post-order quashing) is frequently mixed up with Prohibition (pre-order restraint).
rectification.howToRectify: Remember: Prohibition prevents; Certiorari cures/quashes.

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.statuteRef: Constitution of India (Art. 136)
questions.question: Q73. Special Leave to Appeal to the Supreme Court under Article 136 is:

options.label: D
options.text: Available only against High Court decrees

rectification.principle: Article 136 confers plenary discretionary power on the Supreme Court to grant special leave against any judgment, decree, or order of any court or tribunal in India.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates confuse Article 136 with regular appellate jurisdiction under Articles 132-134.
rectification.howToRectify: Note that military tribunals are the only exclusion under Article 136(2).

questions.subject: Constitutional Law
questions.statuteRef: Constitution of India (Art. 368)
questions.question: Q74. Which judgment established that Parliament cannot alter the Basic Structure of the Constitution under Article 368?

options.label: B
options.text: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala

options.label: C
options.text: Minerva Mills v. Union of India

options.label: D
options.text: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India

rectification.principle: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) propounded the Basic Structure doctrine limiting amending power under Article 368.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Golaknath barred amending Fundamental Rights altogether, whereas Kesavananda introduced Basic Structure.
rectification.howToRectify: Link 1973 Kesavananda Bharati to Article 368 limits.

questions.subject: Criminal Law (BNS / IPC)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita / IPC (Sec. 34 IPC / Sec. 3(5) BNS)
questions.question: Q75. What is the essential requirement for fastening vicarious criminal liability under common intention?

options.label: B
options.text: Prior meeting of minds and participation in criminal act

rectification.principle: Common intention requires pre-arranged plan or prior meeting of minds plus participation in furtherance of that intention.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates mix up common intention (2+ persons) with unlawful assembly common object (5+ persons).
rectification.howToRectify: Compare Sec. 34 (common intention, active participation) with Sec. 149 (common object, 5+ members).

questions.subject: Criminal Law (BNS / IPC)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita / IPC (Sec. 300 IPC / Sec. 101 BNS)
questions.question: Q76. When does culpable homicide NOT amount to murder under the Exception of Grave and Sudden Provocation?

options.label: B
options.text: When the offender is deprived of self-control by grave and sudden provocation not sought as an excuse

options.label: D
options.text: When committed with a licensed weapon

rectification.principle: Exception 1 reduces murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder if the accused loses self-control due to grave and sudden provocation, subject to the three provisos.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Missing the provisos (not sought, not lawful exercise of public power/self-defence) leads to wrong choices.
rectification.howToRectify: Read K.M. Nanavati v. State of Maharashtra for the cooling-off time test.

questions.subject: Criminal Law (BNS / IPC)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita / IPC (Sec. 378 IPC / Sec. 303 BNS)
questions.question: Q77. Dishonest intention at the time of taking movable property out of the possession of another without consent constitutes:

rectification.principle: Theft requires dishonest intention to take movable property out of another person possession without consent.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Criminal misappropriation and CBT involve lawful initial possession, whereas theft is unlawful taking from possession.
rectification.howToRectify: Check whether property was already entrusted (CBT) or taken without consent (Theft).

questions.subject: Criminal Law (BNS / IPC)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita / IPC (Sec. 499 IPC / Sec. 356 BNS)
questions.question: Q78. Which of the following is a valid statutory exception to criminal defamation?

options.label: A
options.text: Imputation made in private correspondence only

options.label: B
options.text: True imputation made for the public good

rectification.principle: Truth alone is not a complete defence in criminal defamation unless it is also made for the public good (First Exception).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: In civil defamation truth alone suffices, but criminal defamation requires truth + public good.
rectification.howToRectify: Memorize the dual test: Truth AND Public Good.

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure (BNSS / CrPC)
questions.statuteRef: BNSS / Code of Criminal Procedure (Sec. 154 CrPC / Sec. 173 BNSS)
questions.question: Q79. In Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of UP, registration of an FIR on receipt of information disclosing a cognizable offence was held to be:

rectification.principle: Registration of FIR is mandatory under Section 154 CrPC / 173 BNSS if information discloses commission of a cognizable offence.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Some exceptions allow preliminary inquiry (matrimonial, commercial, medical negligence), causing confusion about the general rule.
rectification.howToRectify: General rule = mandatory FIR; preliminary inquiry is only for narrow specified categories.

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure (BNSS / CrPC)
questions.statuteRef: BNSS / Code of Criminal Procedure (Sec. 167(2) CrPC / Sec. 187 BNSS)
questions.question: Q80. What is the maximum period of detention beyond which an accused is entitled to default bail when the offence is punishable with death or life imprisonment?

rectification.principle: Default/statutory bail accrues at 90 days for offences punishable with death, life imprisonment, or 10+ years, and 60 days for other offences.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates frequently swap the 60-day and 90-day thresholds.
rectification.howToRectify: 90 days = >=10 years / life / death; 60 days = all other offences.

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure (BNSS / CrPC)
questions.statuteRef: BNSS / Code of Criminal Procedure (Sec. 438 CrPC / Sec. 482 BNSS)
questions.question: Q81. Which courts have concurrent jurisdiction to grant anticipatory bail?

options.label: A
options.text: Magistrate First Class and Sessions Court

options.label: B
options.text: High Court and Court of Session

rectification.principle: Only the High Court and the Court of Session may grant anticipatory bail under Sec. 438 CrPC / Sec. 482 BNSS.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Magistrates grant regular bail under Sec. 437/480, never anticipatory bail.
rectification.howToRectify: Anticipatory bail = Session Court or High Court only.

questions.subject: Criminal Procedure (BNSS / CrPC)
questions.statuteRef: BNSS / Code of Criminal Procedure (Sec. 482 CrPC / Sec. 528 BNSS)
questions.question: Q82. Inherent powers to prevent abuse of the process of any court or secure the ends of justice vest exclusively in the:

rectification.principle: Section 482 CrPC / Section 528 BNSS saves the inherent powers of the High Court alone.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Subordinate criminal courts have no inherent powers analogous to Sec. 151 CPC.
rectification.howToRectify: Compare Sec. 151 CPC (every civil court) vs Sec. 482 CrPC / 528 BNSS (High Court only).

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam / Evidence Act (Sec. 27 IEA / Sec. 23(2) BSA)
questions.question: Q83. How much of an information received from an accused in police custody is admissible when a fact is discovered in consequence?

options.label: B
options.text: Only so much of the information as relates distinctly to the fact thereby discovered

options.label: C
options.text: Only statements signed by two gazetted officers

options.label: D
options.text: None if made to a police officer

rectification.principle: Only the portion of information distinctly relating to the fact discovered is admissible as an exception to the bar on police confessions.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates mistake the rule as admitting the whole confessional narrative.
rectification.howToRectify: Recall Pulukuri Kottaya v. Emperor: only the discovery-linked portion is admissible.

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam / Evidence Act (Sec. 32(1) IEA / Sec. 26(a) BSA)
questions.question: Q84. A dying declaration is admissible in evidence under the principle:

rectification.principle: A person who is about to die is presumed not to lie (nemo moriturus praesumitur mentire).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Latin maxims are often tested directly in AIBE.
rectification.howToRectify: Pair dying declaration with nemo moriturus praesumitur mentire.

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam / Evidence Act (Sec. 115 IEA / Sec. 121 BSA)
questions.question: Q85. When one person has by declaration, act, or omission intentionally caused another to believe a thing to be true and act upon it, which rule applies?

rectification.principle: Section 115 IEA / 121 BSA codifies the rule of estoppel, preventing a party from denying a representation relied upon.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Estoppel (rule of evidence) is often confused with Res Judicata (rule of procedure).
rectification.howToRectify: Estoppel binds representations by a party; Res Judicata binds prior judicial decisions.

questions.subject: Law of Evidence (BSA / IEA)
questions.statuteRef: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam / Evidence Act (Sec. 65B IEA / Sec. 63 BSA)
questions.question: Q86. Admissibility of secondary electronic records requires a certificate as held mandatory in:

options.label: A
options.text: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar v. Kailash Kushanrao Gorantyal

options.label: B
options.text: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India

options.label: C
options.text: Shreya Singhal v. Union of India

options.label: D
options.text: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India

rectification.principle: Arjun Panditrao Khotkar (2020) affirmed that a Sec. 65B(4) certificate is a mandatory condition precedent for secondary electronic evidence.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Earlier conflicting rulings (Shafhi Mohammad) caused confusion before Arjun Panditrao settled the law.
rectification.howToRectify: Associate Sec. 65B(4) / Sec. 63 BSA certificate with Arjun Panditrao Khotkar.

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.statuteRef: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Sec. 11 CPC)
questions.question: Q87. The doctrine of Res Judicata under Section 11 CPC applies when:

options.label: A
options.text: An earlier suit is still pending

options.label: B
options.text: A matter directly and substantially in issue has been heard and finally decided by a competent court

options.label: D
options.text: A suit is withdrawn with liberty

rectification.principle: Section 11 bars re-litigation of matters directly and substantially in issue between the same parties after final adjudication on merits.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Pending earlier suits trigger Section 10 (Res Sub Judice), not Section 11.
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 10 = Stay of pending subsequent suit; Sec. 11 = Bar after final decision.

questions.statuteRef: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Order XXXIX Rules 1-2 CPC)
questions.question: Q88. Which three-pronged test governs the grant of a temporary injunction under Order 39 CPC?

options.label: B
options.text: Prima facie case, Balance of convenience, Irreparable injury

rectification.principle: This question was officially withdrawn by the Bar Council of India in the Final Answer Key.

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.statuteRef: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Sec. 80 CPC)
questions.question: Q89. Before instituting a suit against the Government or a public officer for an official act, a statutory notice period of how many months is required?

rectification.principle: Section 80 CPC mandates a 2-month prior written notice before suing the Government or public officer, subject to urgent leave under Sec. 80(2).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Statutory notice durations differ across Acts (e.g., 2 months in CPC vs 30 days in NI Act).
rectification.howToRectify: Section 80 CPC = 2 months written notice.

questions.subject: Code of Civil Procedure
questions.statuteRef: Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Order VII Rule 11 CPC)
questions.question: Q90. Rejection of a plaint on the ground that it does not disclose a cause of action is governed by:

rectification.principle: Order VII Rule 11 sets out the six mandatory grounds for rejection of a plaint, including lack of cause of action and statutory bar.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Order VI Rule 17 deals with amendment of pleadings, not rejection.
rectification.howToRectify: Order VII Rule 11 = Rejection of plaint (deemed decree under Sec. 2(2)).

questions.subject: Law of Contract & Specific Relief
questions.statuteRef: Indian Contract Act, 1872 / SRA 1963 (Sec. 11 ICA)
questions.question: Q91. In Mohori Bibee v. Dharmodas Ghose, an agreement entered into by a minor was held to be:

rectification.principle: Under Section 11 of the Indian Contract Act, a minor is incompetent to contract, rendering any minor agreement void ab initio.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Unlike coercion or undue influence (voidable), minority makes an agreement void from inception.
rectification.howToRectify: Minors agreements are void ab initio and cannot be ratified.

questions.subject: Law of Contract & Specific Relief
questions.statuteRef: Indian Contract Act, 1872 / SRA 1963 (Sec. 73 ICA)
questions.question: Q92. The rule in Hadley v. Baxendale regarding remoteness of damages is codified in India under:

rectification.principle: Section 73 awards compensation for loss arising naturally in the usual course of things or known to parties as likely to result from breach.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Section 74 deals with liquidated damages/penalty, whereas Section 73 states the general remoteness principle.
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 73 = Unliquidated damages (Hadley v. Baxendale); Sec. 74 = Stipulated sum/penalty.

questions.subject: Law of Contract & Specific Relief
questions.statuteRef: Indian Contract Act, 1872 / SRA 1963 (Sec. 56 ICA)
questions.question: Q93. When an agreement becomes impossible or unlawful to perform after it is made due to an unforeseen supervening event, it becomes void under:

rectification.principle: Section 56 second paragraph renders a contract void upon supervening impossibility or illegality (Doctrine of Frustration).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Commercial hardship alone does not trigger Sec. 56; physical or legal impossibility is required.
rectification.howToRectify: Recall Satyabrata Ghose v. Mugneeram Bangur on Section 56.

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.statuteRef: Hindu Marriage Act / Muslim Law / Succession (Sec. 13B HMA)
questions.question: Q94. Under Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, what is the minimum period of separate living required before filing a petition for divorce by mutual consent?

rectification.principle: Parties must have been living separately for a period of one year or more before presenting a Sec. 13B(1) mutual consent petition.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates confuse the 1-year pre-filing separation with the 6-month cooling-off motion period under Sec. 13B(2).
rectification.howToRectify: 1 year separation before filing; 6 to 18 months window for second motion (waivable per Amardeep Singh).

questions.subject: Family Law
questions.statuteRef: Hindu Marriage Act / Muslim Law / Succession (Sec. 6 HSA 1956 (2005 Amend.))
questions.question: Q95. In Vineeta Sharma v. Rakesh Sharma (2020), the Supreme Court held that a daughter becomes a coparcener by birth:

options.label: A
options.text: Only if her father was alive on 09.09.2005

options.label: B
options.text: Irrespective of whether her father was alive on 09.09.2005

rectification.principle: Daughters hold coparcenary status by birth with equal rights and liabilities regardless of whether the father was alive on 09-09-2005.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Earlier conflicting decisions (Prakash v. Phulavati) required the father to be alive in 2005.
rectification.howToRectify: Vineeta Sharma overruled Prakash v. Phulavati: coparcenary right is by birth.

questions.subject: Professional Ethics & BCI Rules
questions.statuteRef: Advocates Act, 1961 & BCI Rules (Sec. 35 Advocates Act)
questions.question: Q96. Complaints of professional or other misconduct against an advocate are heard in the first instance by:

options.label: B
options.text: The Disciplinary Committee of the State Bar Council

rectification.principle: Under Section 35 of the Advocates Act, the State Bar Council refers misconduct complaints to its Disciplinary Committee.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: BCI hears appeals under Sec. 37 and original complaints only on transfer/revision.
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 35 = State Bar Council DC; Sec. 37 = Appeal to BCI; Sec. 38 = Appeal to Supreme Court.

questions.subject: Professional Ethics & BCI Rules
questions.statuteRef: Advocates Act, 1961 & BCI Rules (Rule 36 BCI Standards)
questions.question: Q97. Under Rule 36 of the Bar Council of India Rules, an advocate is prohibited from:

options.label: A
options.text: Maintaining a factual website with prior intimation

options.label: B
options.text: Soliciting work or advertising directly or indirectly

rectification.principle: Rule 36 prohibits advocates from soliciting work or advertising, subject to the narrow 2008 amendment permitting basic website particulars.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates overlook the distinction between permitted factual website listings and prohibited solicitation.
rectification.howToRectify: Rule 36 = Strict ban on solicitation and commercial advertising.

questions.subject: Law of Torts & Consumer Protection
questions.statuteRef: Law of Torts / Motor Vehicles / CPA 2019 (M.C. Mehta Rule)
questions.question: Q98. In M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak), the Supreme Court evolved the principle of Absolute Liability, which differs from Rylands v. Fletcher because:

options.label: A
options.text: It applies only to public sector units

options.label: B
options.text: It admits no exceptions such as Act of God or third-party act

options.label: C
options.text: It limits compensation to statutory caps

rectification.principle: Absolute Liability holds enterprises engaged in hazardous or inherently dangerous activities strictly liable with zero exceptions.
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Strict liability (Rylands) allows exceptions like vis major; Absolute Liability allows none.
rectification.howToRectify: Absolute Liability = Strict Liability minus all Rylands v. Fletcher exceptions.

questions.subject: Law of Torts & Consumer Protection
questions.statuteRef: Law of Torts / Motor Vehicles / CPA 2019 (CPA 2019 Sec. 34)
questions.question: Q99. Under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019, the District Commission has pecuniary jurisdiction where the value of goods or services paid as consideration does not exceed:

rectification.principle: Under the 2021 Rules notified under CPA 2019, District Commission jurisdiction is up to Rs. 50 Lakhs (State: 50L to 2 Cr; National: above 2 Cr).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: CPA 1986 limits (20L) and original 2019 Act text (1 Cr) were revised by the 2021 Pecuniary Jurisdiction Rules.
rectification.howToRectify: Remember revised 2021 limits: District <= 50L; State > 50L to 2 Cr; National > 2 Cr (based on consideration paid).

questions.subject: Alternative Dispute Resolution
questions.statuteRef: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (Sec. 34 A&C Act)
questions.question: Q100. What is the standard limitation period for filing an application to set aside an arbitral award under Section 34(3)?

options.label: C
options.text: 3 months (extendable by 30 days on sufficient cause)

rectification.principle: Section 34(3) prescribes 3 months from receipt of the award, extendable by at most 30 days on sufficient cause, but not thereafter (Sec. 5 Limitation Act excluded).
rectification.whyMistakeHappens: Candidates confuse 3 months with 90 days or assume Section 5 Limitation Act applies indefinitely.
rectification.howToRectify: Sec. 34(3): 3 months + max 30 days grace; Popular Construction excludes Sec. 5 Limitation Act.
